/itineraryStops/0/smartNotes/tip.source_en: Arrive 30 minutes before booked DMZ shuttle time for ID check. Bring physical passport (digital photos and Alien Registration Card alone may not be accepted at the Civilian Control Line for foreigners). Skip the amusement park unless traveling with young children.

/itineraryStops/0/smartNotes/facilities.source_en: 1st-floor tourism center cheap snack stalls (corn dogs, sausage rice cake, dumplings); 2nd-floor sit-down restaurants. Annyeong cafe at Pyeonghwa-Nuri serves teas. North Korean currency for sale as souvenirs (legal collectible).

/itineraryStops/0/whyOnRoute.source_en: Starting at Imjingak sets the emotional and historical tone for the day before crossing into the DMZ proper, where photography and free movement are both restricted. It is also the mandatory tour-staging point — passport ID checks happen here, and the DMZ shuttle bus departs from here onward to the 3rd Tunnel and ⟦G0⟧. The combination of monuments, exhibits, and panoramic Imjin River vista lets the driver-guide compress 50+ years of separated-family history (Korean War, 1953 POW repatriation, ongoing Mangbaedan ritual every Lunar New Year and Chuseok) into a single 30-40 minute walk before the day shifts to the more politically intense 3rd Tunnel and ⟦G0⟧ zones — where photography and free movement are heavily restricted. Imjingak is also the **mandatory tour-staging point** for any DMZ Peace & Security Tourist Program: passport ID checks happen here, the dedicated DMZ shuttle bus departs from here, and individual-vehicle access beyond Unification Bridge is prohibited under the Civilian Control Line.

/itineraryStops/0/description.source_en:
About 70 minutes north of Seoul along National Highway 1, Imjingak Peace Park sits 7 km from the Military Demarcation Line on the banks of the Imjin River. Built in 1972 to console the displaced families separated by the Korean War, the park draws around 1.2 million visitors annually and serves as the staging ground for all Paju-si DMZ Peace Tours. 

The grounds gather the most powerful symbols of the divided peninsula in one place: the Mangbaedan Altar where Korean families with hometowns in the North perform ancestral rites bowing northward each Lunar New Year and Chuseok; the Freedom Bridge — a former rail bridge temporarily built in 1953 to repatriate 12,773 prisoners of war returning from the North; and the bullet-ridden Jangdan Station steam locomotive (registered Cultural Heritage 2004) on the destroyed Gyeongui rail line, a visual reminder of how long the border has been closed. 

Adjacent to the original Imjingak Pavilion, the Pyeonghwa-Nuri Park section opened in 2005 with a 20,000-person performance lawn (host of the annual MBC Gayo Daejejeon since 2006), the Bell of Peace (built 2000), Windy Hill with thousands of colorful pinwheels, and Dolmuji unification-prayer rock cairns. 

An on-site gondola crosses the Imjin River with stations on both banks, while a small Pyeonghwa Land amusement park operates year-round — the latter providing a sometimes-jarring contrast to the memorial atmosphere. 

The site is **officially designated 'Imjingak National Tourist Site'** by Paju City — address **177 Imjingak-ro, Paju-si, Gyeonggi-do**. Beyond the main monument cluster, the broader National Tourist Site complex includes Unification Park (with the US Army 187th Airborne Combat Team Monument and Burma Aung San Martyrdom Memorial), the Korea 6.25 War Abductees Memorial Hall, and the Peace Bell built in 2000 for the new millennium. Average visitor count exceeds 10,000 per day on holidays.
